A big reason why this is important: hushmail a few years ago were an anonymous email provider, but were compelled by the NSA to change their code to insert a backdoor of sorts, that would basically intercept and record your private decryption key. This was used to gain access to a number of individuals accounts, decrypt their data, and hand it over to the NSA / FBI.

Whilst I'm sure these individuals were being very naughty, it basically showed the rest of us that even a 'secure' email provider can be completely compromised without us being any the wiser. By open-sourcing their code, as long as someone is keeping an eye on code changes, Tutanota essentially protect their service and their users from this kind of backdoor.

Great question and I wish I knew the answer. I had just assumed after being a FOSS advocate for a long time that one could compile the code and compare the binaries, but I wouldn't know how you do that for web applications.

Ok I've done a bit more research, and it seems that Tutanota does 100% of the encryption locally, so for example:

  1. Open app / website
  2. Enter password 'hunter2'
  3. This is hashed to retrieve your encrypted data from the server (so the server only sees something like "asdf978asdf976asdf78")
  4. Back on your local machine now, your data is a load of nonsense but you've got it stored locally in memory
  5. The app uses your password as above 'hunter2' with a decryption algorithm to convert your data back to readable text
  6. You can read and write emails

So because of this, you can build the service, then verify that the local or client side actions match the known good version from the source code.

You can't guarantee that the server-side code matches the source code, however, that shouldn't matter because you can verify that your local client-side DOES match the source code, and therefore you KNOW that your client isn't sending 'hunter2' to the server at any point.

Here's the quote from the tutanota account on reddit:

The encryption of Tutanota happens locally on the client within your browser or app. The code for this is on github for tech experts to check it or to run their version of Tutanota locally: https://github.com/tutao/tutanota

If you run a service that grants privacy while being within direct reach of a government that allows things like that, and there are a few around these days, then the service was never able to provide what they offered.

That the inevitable happened then was just the logical consequence of the original mistake.

Its not a matter of technology, its a matter of physics. Your resolution is limited by the wave length of the light in relation to the iris of your detector. So if you want to see visible light from 100 miles away, to get the same as the black bird you need...

We'll say the black bird camera had a 6 inch iris.
We'll say the cig pack is 2 inches.
So 6/3 = x/100. Or 3x = 600. Or x = 200. So to get a comparable image from 100 miles as 3 miles, you'd need an iris that is about 200 inches across, or about 16.6 feet across.
If the Black Bird's camera had a 3 inch iris, then the 100 mile away satellite would need an iris about 33 feet across.

That's garbage. Sensitivity and sensor size do not change with zoom. This should be very obvious from the fact that replaceable lens cameras have exactly the same sensitivity and sensor size while the zoom changes. What does change is light gathering - the more you zoom, the less light gathered. This is partly compensated by the stabilisation, however. Sharpness suffers a bit too. Also, having a non-replaceable lens does not make a camera obsolete. Lenses don't age much at all. The main part of a camera that obsolesces is the sensor, and that isn't replaceable in any camera.
